These match the fill modes of Tinkercad's SVG import: default, outer line and inner line. “Wider” keeps the area filled and grows it by the line width all round, with sharp, round or bevelled corners: a base layer under a logo for a multicolour print, which the stroke outside alone would only give as a ring. “Silhouette (No Holes)” leaves out every outline lying inside another: holes and whatever lies in them. Only the outer outline stays. Together with “Stroke Outside” it makes a cookie cutter: import an SVG twice, once with the silhouette as an area for the base and once with the silhouette and 1 to 2 mm of stroke outside as the wall. The switch is in the “Stroke” panel in sketch mode as well. Fillets and chamfers on the edges go when the body is built again, as when the sketch is edited.

An extruded sketch has vertical walls. A stamp, an embossing die or a punch wants slanted ones, outside and inside, with the same wall thickness all the way. Layerling has no draft angle for an extrusion, but for plain outlines the “Taper” gets you there. One way that works: Draw the outline with the hole it needs and make a body of it. Duplicate the body (Ctrl+D). On the first body, switch on “Silhouette (No Holes)”, so the hole is filled, and give it a wider bottom than top with “Taper”. On the copy, open its sketch again and delete the outer outline, so that only the outline of the hole is left. Finish the sketch, switch the body to “Hole” and give it a narrower bottom than top with “Taper”. Move the hole into the first body, where the hole was, and group the two. The walls now slope outside and inside. Taper scales the whole outline, so this is exact for plain shapes, where you can choose the sizes so the walls run parallel, and only an approximation for fine details such as lettering.

With “Add Image” you put a photo or a drawing under the sketch and trace it. You can set its size, opacity and position. Once the picture sits right, lock it with L so you do not move it by accident while drawing. A locked image is out of the way: clicks go through it, so you can pick lines and points on top of it and drag a frame over them. To select it again, for example to unlock it, Alt+click it. If its settings at the right edge cover the picture, drag them away by their title bar; a double-click on it docks them again. Under “Align” you line up a photo that was not taken straight: “Rotation”: Turn the picture about its centre, with the round handle above its frame or as a number in degrees. With Shift the handle snaps in 15° steps. “To X = 0” and “To Y = 0”: put the picture's centre on X = 0 or Y = 0. For a revolve, X = 0 is the axis, so the picture then lies symmetric about it. “Calibrate”: Click two points in the picture whose distance you know, the ends of a ruler or a known diameter, and type the real distance. The picture is scaled evenly so that distance is right; the first point stays where it was. “Crop”: The handles on the frame now crop the picture instead of scaling it; what is cut away stays stored and comes back with “Show whole picture” or when a handle is pulled out again. All four touch the reference only, never the sketch.

Key Effect Esc end the line chain, clear the selection Delete delete the selected element Ctrl+C copy the selection Ctrl+X cut the selection Ctrl+V paste Ctrl+D duplicate the selection Ctrl+Z undo Shift while drawing: snap the line in 15° steps; while dragging: keep movement on one axis digit, <, Tab, Enter while drawing: type and set the length and angle of the next line R rotate the closed sketch by 45° L lock or unlock the template image Tip: Draw as few points as needed. An outline with a few well-placed points gives a smoother body than a tangle of many.
Raised or engraved lettering in seven typefaces or one of your own, and if you like along a circular arc, such as on a coin, a lid or a ring.

Choose “Text” in the shape library and place it. In the “Text” field on the right, type what it should say. The settings below: “Font”: Seven typefaces are available: Multilanguage, Sans, Serif, Script, Monospace, Rounded and Stencil (letters made of straight lines). New text starts in Sans. Accented letters such as ä, ö, ü, é and the € sign are in every typeface. Fonts of your own come on top, see Your own fonts below. “Letter size”: How big the letters are, seen from above; “Height” sets how thick they are. “Height”: How far the lettering stands out from the surface. “Bevel”: Rounds the letter edges so they look softer. With “Segments” you decide in how many steps. Size: You set the length and width of the line as with any shape. Drag the handles or type the dimensions. Text is at first a single body. If you want to treat the letters individually, click “Separate Parts”. Then every letter is a shape of its own. The edges of text can be chamfered or filleted too, straight or curved, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies. Use small sizes such as 0.2 to 0.5 mm, because the strokes of the letters are narrow.

Besides the seven built-in fonts you can use any font of your own: a font file from your computer or, in Chrome and Edge, a font installed on your computer. Choose “Your own fonts …” at the bottom of “Font”. The “Your own fonts” window opens. “Choose a font file …” takes a TrueType file (.ttf), an OpenType file (.otf) or a WOFF file (.woff). You can also simply drag the file into the window. On Windows the installed fonts live in the Fonts folder (C:\Windows\Fonts). The browser's file dialog hides it. Open it in Explorer instead and drag the font into the “Your own fonts” window. Fonts installed for you alone live in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Fonts, which the file dialog shows too. On a Mac fonts live in /Library/Fonts and ~/Library/Fonts. “Font from the computer …” lists the fonts installed on your computer. The first time, the browser asks whether layerling may read them. The search field finds a font quickly, a click takes it. If a text is selected, it gets the new font at once. Otherwise the font shows up under “Font” in the “Your own fonts” group, and “Use” in the window puts it on the selected texts. Fonts of your own work like the built-in ones: text on a circular arc, chamfers and fillets on the edges and the STEP export all work the same. Letters a font lacks are taken from Sans.

Arabic, Persian, Urdu and Hebrew are written right to left: the first letter stands on the right, and in a mixed text such as "Name عربي" only the Arabic word runs backwards, digits stay as usual. Arabic letters join their neighbours the way the script asks, and lam-alef becomes a ligature. This needs a font that has these letters; the built-in ones do not. Add one of your own, such as Arial, Tahoma or Segoe UI on Windows, or a free one such as Noto Naskh Arabic, Noto Sans Arabic or Amiri. Vowel marks sit on the letter they belong to. Text on a circular arc, outline, silhouette, layers and name tags work with it as with any other text.

Browser Choose a font file Font from the computer Chrome and Edge on a computer, the installed layerling app too yes yes, after the browser asks Firefox yes no Safari on a Mac yes no Tablet and phone yes, from the device's files no Web pages may not simply read the installed fonts. Only Chrome and Edge have a permission for it, and only on secure pages, over https as on layerling.com. When layerling runs over http, say on your own server or as a Docker install in your home network, “Font from the computer …” is missing; drag the font over from Explorer then. In the other browsers you choose the font file from the fonts folder, with the same result. If you declined the question in Chrome or Edge, allow it again in the site settings, behind the padlock to the left of the address. layerling cannot read WOFF2 files (there is almost always a TTF or OTF version), font collections (.ttc, several fonts in one file) or colour emoji fonts. From very large fonts, such as Chinese ones, layerling takes the first 8000 characters. A variable font is read in its default setting, usually the regular weight. Some fonts, script and variable fonts above all, draw a letter from strokes that overlap. layerling merges them into one clean outline when it reads the font, so the body stays printable. Such letters are then made of very short straight pieces instead of curves; it does not show.

A font of your own stays in this browser on this computer. Another browser or another computer does not know it until you add it there too. Clearing the browser's site data clears the fonts as well. In the “Your own fonts” window the bin removes a font from the browser. Your designs lose nothing by it, as the next section shows.

h: Passing on designs with a font of your own
t: A design does not store the font file, only the outlines of the letters its texts use, those in earlier steps of the history included. If a text says "Hello", only H, e, l and o travel with it. That holds for every way a design is saved: in the browser, on your own server, as a .lyl file and in “Custom shapes”. So: The design opens correctly anywhere, also on a computer without the font. The texts look the same and can be moved, turned, scaled and filleted. New letters need the font. If someone without the font types a letter the design did not bring along, layerling draws it from Sans. Under “Font” the font is then marked “only the design's letters”. Adding the font file brings back every letter. Exports hold geometry only. STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP and SVG contain bodies and outlines, no font. Older layerling versions do not know fonts of one's own yet and draw such texts in Multilanguage. Licences: Fonts are protected by copyright, and their licence says what you may do with them. The embedded letter outlines are what PDF files take along from a font, and most licences allow that. Some commercial fonts, though, forbid passing on even single letters. Before you pass on or publish a design with a font of your own, check the font's licence. Free fonts such as those from Google Fonts (mostly under the SIL Open Font License) can be passed on without worry. For a printed part or an exported STL it does not matter: they hold no font any more, only geometry.

Raised: Place the text on the surface and group it with the body. It grows out as a relief. Engraved: Switch the text to “Hole”, let it reach a little into the surface and group it with the body. The letters are then engraved. For lettering on a side face, first put the workplane on that face, see View and workplane.

A text need not be built as filled letters. “Fill” in the properties offers the same choice as Tinkercad: “Filled”: the letters as they are. “Outline”: a line along the outline of the letters, half inside and half outside it. “Outer line”: a line round the outside of the letters. “Inner line”: a line on the inside of the letters. With a line chosen, two settings appear right under the list: “Line Width” sets how thick the line is, “Corners” how it goes round the corners (“Round”, “Bevel” or “Sharp”). The rarer settings are under “More”: “Silhouette (No Holes)” leaves out the holes in O, A or e, and “Wider (base for a multicolour print)” keeps the letters filled and makes them thicker by the line width all round; letters that touch grow into one piece. With a line outside, a centred line or "Wider" the box of the text grows, while the letters keep their size. “Bevel” and “Segments” exist for filled letters only.

A name tag for a multicolour print is a text in layers: the letters on top, under them the same text a little wider in a second colour, at the bottom a plate without holes in a third. layerling makes it in one click: A new name tag: choose “Name tag” in the shape library and place it. It says "Name" in white letters on a red rim and a dark plate. From a text: select the text and click “Make layers” at the top of its settings. All settings of the tag are in the card “Name tag”, at the top of the settings: “Text” and “Font”, fonts of your own too. The tag grows with the words. “Letter size”: how tall the capital letters are, in mm. All layers follow and stay lined up. “Layers”: one row per layer, from the top down. Each row has the colour (click the coloured square), how much wider the layer is than the letters, its height and “No holes”, which fills the holes in letters such as O and A. “Corners” sets how a wider layer goes round the corners of the letters: “Round”, “Bevel” or “Sharp”. The top row is the letters themselves. + adds a layer at the bottom, – takes the bottom layer away. A tag has two to six layers. “Key ring hole”: gives the bottom layer a straight tab with a round end and a hole for a key ring; the tab grows with the hole. A 3 mm hole, the default, makes a tab 6.5 mm wide that sticks out 6.75 mm, the hole's edge 2 mm from the edge of the bottom layer. Choose the “Hole diameter” and the “Side”: “Left”, “Right” or “Top”. The hole goes through every layer it touches, and the tab moves along when you change the words, the letter size or the font. “Letter edge”: rounds or chamfers the top edge of the letters on the top layer, the way a printed tag is finished: “None”, “Round” or “Chamfer”, with the “Edge size” (0.4 mm to start with, at most as high as the layer). It works for every font and word. The edge is part of the letters' mesh, so the edge tool takes such a text as a mesh, which for a text this fine is heavy; pick the edge here instead. Every change shows at once. The tag is a bundle: it moves as one, and each layer stays a body of its own in its own colour, the way a slicer needs them for a multicolour print. To round or bevel the edges of one layer, click “Edit bundle” and pick the layer, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies.

Type the names into “Name list”, one per line, up to a hundred. The button below says how many tags it will make, for example "Make 12 name tags". Every tag gets the same layers, letter size and key ring hole and is an object of its own; they are laid out in rows below the first, 5 mm apart. A plain text has the name list too, further down in its settings.

An icon tag is the same tag with an SVG icon instead of letters: a heart, a cloud, a club's logo. The icon on top, under it the same outline a little wider in a second colour, at the bottom a plate without holes. A new icon tag: choose “Icon tag” in the shape library. A small window opens: click “Browse…”, pick an SVG file, check the picture, type the “Width (mm)” of the icon and click “OK”. The tag stands in the middle of the plate, in the same layers as a new name tag. From a sketch body: an imported SVG, or a sketch you drew, has “Make layers” at the top of its settings. The card “Icon tag” at the top of the settings holds: “Another SVG…”: puts another SVG's icon on the tag; the layers and the width stay as they are. “Width”: how wide the icon on top is, in mm. All layers follow and stay lined up. “Layers”: the rows as on a name tag - colour, how much wider, “Corners”, height and “No holes”, + and –, two to six layers. The top row is the icon itself. “Count”: how many tags you want, 1 to 100. “As many as fit” works it out from the plate of the printer chosen in the settings, for small logos a full plate. The button below makes them, 5 mm apart, laid out on the middle of the plate; the first is the tag itself. The SVG needs closed outlines; a drawing of open lines only cannot become a tag. A sketch body whose fill is a line keeps it: the area of that line is the icon.

Should the lettering not run straight but follow the edge of a coin, a lid or a ring? For that there is the setting “On arc”. Text follows a circle. All letters stand on one common line. Once you switch it on, the text runs along the circle. All letters stand on the same baseline, as evenly as with normal text. There are four settings: “Arc radius” (5 to 500 mm): The radius of the circle the letters' baseline runs on. “Letter size”: How tall the letters are. It no longer depends on the width of the shape. “Along the bottom”: Moves the text from the top of the circle to its bottom. The letters then point with their heads to the centre. “Upside down”: Turns only the letters over so you can read them from the other side. The text stays in its place on the circle. The centre of the circle is the centre of the shape. That is why aligning works as usual: if you centre the text with a cylinder or ring, it sits exactly concentric on it. When you pull a handle, radius and letter size grow together, so the lettering is not distorted. Tip: At the top of the circle the letters stand outside the baseline; with “Along the bottom” they stand inside, heads towards the centre. For the lettering to fit on a disc, the radius plus the letter size should be smaller than the disc's radius.

Screws, nuts and tapped holes that fit together, plus gear, spring, bent tube, dovetail, teardrop hole, counterbore and countersink. Besides the basic shapes, the library contains some parts that would be tedious to put together yourself. All of them can be changed afterwards in their settings.

Choose “Thread” in the shape library. Under “Type” you decide what it should be: “Threaded rod”: a cylinder with thread, for example a screw without a head. “Screw”: with a head. You choose the “Head”: “Socket head”, “Countersunk” or “Hex head”. “Nut”: the matching nut. “Tapped hole”: a tapped hole. It is a hole. Drag it into a part, group both, and the part has an internal thread. A screw with a cylinder head. On the right: kind and head shape, further down size, pitch and profile. You pick the size under “Size” from a list: metric from M2 to M12, the inch sizes UNC and UNF from No. 4 to 1 inch, and the pipe threads G1/16 to G4. If you choose “Custom”, you set “Diameter” and “Pitch” yourself. For an inch size or a G size the field asks for “Threads per inch” instead of the pitch in millimetres. The list groups the sizes by series, and a line under the field names the series of the size you picked, with examples you know from everyday life: M, metric coarse: the ISO metric coarse thread to ISO 261, as on standard screws and nuts. UNC, US inch coarse: the camera and tripod screw is 1/4"-20 UNC (ISO 1222), larger tripod heads use 3/8"-16 UNC. UNF, US inch fine: the same diameters as UNC with a finer pitch (ASME B1.1). G, pipe thread: a shower hose connects with G1/2, a washing-machine inlet hose with G3/4. A garden tap ends in G3/4, smaller taps in G1/2; that is where the tap connector of a click-on hose system screws on. The G sizes are the parallel Whitworth pipe threads to ISO 228-1, found on fittings for water, gas, hydraulics and pneumatics. The size names the pipe, not the thread: a G1 measures 33.249 mm across the thread. Choosing a G size sets the profile to “Whitworth (55°)”, and choosing a metric or inch size sets it back to “V-thread (ISO)”. A “Trapezoidal” or “Round” profile you picked yourself stays. The standard only defines the thread, so the head of a screw and a nut on a G size get the same proportions as on a diameter you set yourself. The tapered pipe threads R, Rc and Rp are not included. More settings: “Direction”: “Right-hand” or “Left-hand”. “Profile”: “V-thread (ISO)” is the standard profile of metric and inch threads, “Whitworth (55°)” that of the G pipe threads: 55° with rounded crests and roots. “Trapezoidal” and “Round” have flat crests and roots. That usually prints more reliably because no thin tips result. “Custom (trapezoid)”: A trapezoid you shape yourself, with a flat crest and a flat root of the same width. “Flank angle” is the angle between the two flanks of a tooth: 60° is the sharp V thread, 30° the trapezoid thread, and at 90° or less no flank is flatter than 45°, so the thread prints without supports. “Thread depth” and “Core diameter” are one measure said two ways: the core diameter is the diameter minus twice the depth, and changing one changes the other. A new own profile starts with the V thread's depth at 60°. The depth has limits that depend on the angle and the pitch: not shallower than a tenth of the pitch, not deeper than 40 % of the diameter, and not so deep that the two flanks take more than nine tenths of the pitch. If you change the pitch, the depth follows in proportion; if you scale the thread, so does the depth. The play and the chamfers work as with the other profiles. Through the MCP bridge the profile is custom with threadFlankAngle and threadDepth. “Clearance (XY)”: For nut and tapped hole, the room that makes sure a printed pair really turns. The coarser your printer works, the more clearance the pair needs. It is the extra room across the whole diameter, and the gap between the flanks of a V thread is only about half of it, so a printed pair needs more than you might expect: new nuts start at 0.4 mm, 0.3 is tight and 0.5 loose. Print a test pair first. Rods and screws have a clearance of their own here, which makes the bolt that much thinner in diameter. It is set to 0. Which side gets the room depends on what you pair: Printed screw and printed nut: leave the screw at 0 and give the nut the room (the 0.4 mm it starts with). Real screw in a printed nut or tapped hole: the printed side takes all of it, so the nut keeps its 0.4 mm. A tighter 0.3 mm is worth a test if the screw wobbles. Printed screw in a real nut: the real nut has no play, so the screw has to be thinner: 0.3 to 0.4 mm here, as much as a printed nut would have. “Play along the axis (Z)”: For nut and tapped hole, the play along the axis, on top of the “Clearance (XY)”. Every tooth of the nut gets this much thinner, the diameter stays as it is. The reason: the “Clearance (XY)” works on the diameter only and opens the flanks of a V thread to about 0.58 of its value. Anyone who wants air between the flanks has to open the diameter wide and gets sideways slop for it. The play along the axis sets the two apart. It is set to 0, so a saved thread does not change, and it goes up to a fifth of the pitch at most, because above that nothing would be left of the nut's teeth. The field exists for nut and tapped hole only; rod and screw keep their own clearance. More below under "Threads for 3D printing". “Chamfer, top end”, “Chamfer, bottom end”, “Head chamfer” and “Rim chamfer”: Chamfers at the ends so the thread starts cleanly and the head has no sharp edge. Each end of a rod, nut or tapped hole has its own chamfer, so the top can be long and the bottom short or none. A screw has only one at its tip, labelled “Chamfer”. On a nut or tapped hole the chamfer is the room the mouth opens beyond the outer diameter; the cone runs at 45 degrees on down to the thread core, so no ledge is left at the outer diameter. Switching a thread between “Threaded rod” and “Tapped hole” keeps its length. A nut and a screw start from their standard measures. “Quality”: How finely the thread is calculated. Higher is more exact, but slower. Printed threads are a topic of their own. Make the screw-and-nut pair as a test first before you print a large part, and adjust the clearance to your printer.

A printed thread needs air in two places, and they act differently: Clearance in the diameter (“Clearance (XY)”): makes the nut wider. The screw then has half the value as air on each side, 0.2 mm at 0.4 mm. The thread turns easily, but the screw can wobble sideways. Play along the axis (“Play along the axis (Z)”): makes the teeth of the nut thinner. The screw can then move back and forth along the axis by that value when it is not tightened. There is no extra air to the side for it. Together they make the gap between the flanks: about 0.58 times the clearance in the diameter plus the play along the axis. An example for a 0.3 mm gap: it used to take 0.5 mm in the diameter, that is 0.25 mm of air on each side. Now 0.2 mm in the diameter (0.1 mm on each side) and 0.2 mm along the axis do it, and the gap is 0.32 mm. Consequences to know The screw has play along the axis. Without load it can move back and forth by that value. For fastenings, lids and housings that does not matter; for a lead screw that has to position exactly it does, so keep it small or at 0 there. The nut's teeth get thinner. With 0.3 mm at a pitch of 1.75 mm every tooth is almost a third thinner at its middle and so clearly less strong. For heavily loaded parts take a coarser thread instead. More to calculate. The tooth shape gets extra points, so the thread has more triangles and takes a little longer to compute. No true arc in the STEP export for the Whitworth profile. A “Whitworth (55°)” thread with play along the axis goes to the edge tool and the STEP export as a tooth shape made of straight pieces, not with the true circular arcs. At 0 everything stays as before. Tips A test pair first. A screw and a nut, each only 4 to 6 mm tall, take a few minutes. Print three pairs with different play side by side and take the one that turns easily and does not wobble. Start with values that often fit. Clearance in the diameter 0.2 to 0.3 mm and play along the axis 0.2 mm. If the screw wobbles sideways, lower the clearance in the diameter; if it jams, raise the play along the axis. If you would rather do without the play along the axis, use 0.4 mm in the diameter as before. The play along the axis should be at least one layer height. What lies below one layer the printer does not resolve. With a layer height of 0.2 mm, 0.2 mm is a good start; with 0.1 mm, less is enough. Print screw and nut upright. The axis points up, so every turn lies in whole layers and the flanks come out clean. Lying down, the flanks sag. Fine pitches are hard. Below about 1 mm of pitch the turns often fuse. A coarser thread, or a “Trapezoidal” profile with flat crests, prints more reliably than a fine V thread. Avoid thin tips. The V thread has a narrow tip that the printer hardly hits with its nozzle width. The “Trapezoidal” and “Round” profiles have flatter teeth. Deburr and run it in. The first turns are often stiff because small remains of the print stand on the flanks. Turn it back and forth a few times and it runs easier. The chamfer at the start helps threading it in. Another printer or filament. The play depends on the printer, the material and the nozzle. Print the test pair again when you change either. The edge tool takes a thread as its exact body. You can chamfer or round the part that carries it with the thread already in place, or the rims of a screw head, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies. Working out a thread's edges takes a while: a few seconds for an M6, about half a minute for a G1/2 pipe thread. The quickest way to break the edge of a screw head is still the head chamfer in the properties.

“Gear” comes as “Spur gear”, “Helical gear”, “Herringbone gear” and “Bevel gear”, and as “Ring gear” and “Rack” (further down). New gears have “Involute” under “Tooth Shape”: teeth with involute flanks, as gear generators and engineering use them. Such teeth roll cleanly on each other. You set the number of “Teeth” and the “Module (mm)”, and the size follows: the outside diameter is module × (teeth + 2), the pitch circle module × teeth. New gears start at module 2. Two gears mesh when they have the same module and the same “Pressure Angle” (usually 20°) and their centres stand (teeth + teeth) × module / 2 apart. Select both gears and the properties panel gives that centre distance and how far apart the centres are now. If a tooth then meets a tooth instead of a gap, turn one of the gears by half a tooth, which is 180° divided by its number of teeth. “Backlash” takes a little off the teeth so a printed pair does not bind. The value is for the pair, and each gear takes half of it; 0.2 mm is a good start, 0 gives the exact gear. Below the base circle the flank runs straight down to the root and is not undercut as a cutter would do it. That suits printing, but a very small pinion below about 17 teeth may rub slightly at the root. A helical gear adds the “Helix Angle”. With involute teeth it is the true helix angle on the pitch circle: two helical gears mesh when they have the same module and the same angle, one positive and the other negative. The “Herringbone gear” is two helical halves turning opposite ways: the teeth run one way up to half the height and back after it, like an arrow. That has two advantages for 3D printing: the gear centres itself on its shaft, and it has no axial thrust, because the forces of the two halves cancel. A helical gear, in contrast, pushes sideways along its axis. You set the “Helix Angle” and the “Helix quality” as for the helical gear; the angle applies to each half. Two herringbone gears mesh when they have the same module and the same angle with opposite signs, one positive and the other negative. There is no groove in the middle, as on milled herringbone gears: the two halves run into each other without a step. The edge tool and the STEP export take the herringbone gear as a triangle mesh, not as an exact body. The bevel gear takes the involute teeth and makes them smaller towards its top. That is an approximation, not an exactly worked out bevel pair. “Round” are round teeth made of arcs, like Tinkercad's Useful gear: tip and gap run into each other without a corner. Small gears print more forgivingly that way and turn more easily, and on a knob the teeth make a pleasant grip. Round teeth are set by “Teeth”, “Module (mm)” and “Backlash” too; they have no pressure angle. They stand lower than involute teeth, so the outside diameter is module × (teeth + 1.2). Round gears with the same module mesh, at the same centre distance as involute ones; with an involute gear they do not fit. “Simple” are the straight teeth every gear had so far. There you set “Tooth Size” and “Tooth Width” by hand. Older designs keep them until you change the tooth shape. All three tooth shapes have the “Center Hole”. The “Ring gear” has its teeth pointing in: a ring that a smaller gear runs inside, like the outer wheel of a planetary set. You set it like an involute or round gear by “Teeth”, “Module (mm)” and “Backlash”, plus the “Rim”, the ring outside the teeth. Its outside diameter is module × (teeth + 2.5) plus twice the rim, with round teeth module × (teeth + 1.7). A gear of the same module runs in it when its centre stands (ring teeth − its teeth) × module / 2 from the ring's centre; select both and the properties panel gives that distance. For a planetary set, ring teeth = sun teeth + 2 × planet teeth, for example 30 = 12 + 2 × 9. A ring gear has no centre hole, it is the ring itself. Between 26 and 33 teeth its tips are up to a quarter module shorter, because a tiny edge would otherwise form at the base circle; meshing is not affected. The “Rack” is the gear of endless radius: a bar with teeth along one side, whose flanks are straight lines at the pressure angle with involute teeth. Its width (along X) is teeth × pitch, the pitch being π × module, so racks of one module line up end to end, each end falling in a gap. Its length (along Y) is the thickness of the bar and free, as long as the teeth and half a millimetre of bar fit in. The teeth point to the front, towards the viewer of the home view; turn the rack as you need it. A gear of the same module rolls on it when its centre stands its teeth × module / 2 in front of the pitch line; the pitch line lies a module behind the tooth tips, 0.6 module with round teeth. Ring gear and rack come with involute and with round teeth, not with simple ones; switching the gear type keeps the module. The edge tool and the STEP export take every gear as its exact body, involute flanks as smooth curves. A helical gear on an oval footprint stays a triangle mesh, and so does a helical gear with involute teeth from about 31 teeth. Small teeth limit how far edges can be rounded: on a gear with simple teeth, 30 mm across with 12 teeth the flat between two teeth at the foot is only about 0.65 mm wide, so rounding every edge works up to about 0.5 mm, and on a bevel gear, whose top is smaller, up to about 0.4 mm. A helical gear's teeth lean, which narrows that flat across its slanted edges: the larger the helix angle against the gear's height, the smaller the rounding that fits. The edges of its two flat ends can be rounded, but chamfering just those edges fails in the CAD kernel; round them, or chamfer all edges together at a smaller size, such as 0.2 mm.

The “Spring” has “Turns” and a “Wire”. Together with the height they decide how soft the spring is. “Winding” sets which way the wire runs: “Right-hand” like a usual compression spring, or “Left-hand”. The edge tool and the STEP export take a spring as its exact body: a round wire along a helix, cut square at both ends. You can round or chamfer those two wire ends, for instance.

A “Bent Tube” consists of up to twelve sections: a straight piece followed by a bend. For each you set the “Straight length”, the “Bend angle”, the “Bend radius” and the “Roll angle”. The section you are editing is lit up in orange on the tube, so you can follow the order. A roll angle of 0° bends within the plane of the workplane, at 90° the tube bends upward. The profile can be round, square, hexagonal or octagonal, the inside likewise, or fully solid. If the tube runs into itself, layerling warns you.

The “Loft” joins one outline at the bottom to another at the top, like a loft in Fusion: a hose adapter from one diameter to another, a square fan onto a round duct, a stand that turns round towards the top. For each end you pick “Bottom Outline” and “Top Outline”: “Circle / ellipse”, “Rectangle” with “Bottom Corner Radius”, or “Polygon” with its number of corners, plus the width and length of each end and the height. “Top Offset in Width” and “Top Offset in Length” move the top end sideways for a slanted transition; the bottom end stays where it is. “Wall Thickness (0 = solid)” turns the solid body into a tube open at the top and the bottom. The opening is smaller by the wall at both ends, measured across; where the wall slants it is a little thinner. Drag the frame bigger and both ends grow along, while the corner radius and the wall keep their size. “Smooth transition (%)” makes the transition smooth. At 0 the sides run straight from the bottom to the top, as on a cone. At 100 they leave both ends straight up and change their size in between along an S-curve: a hose adapter that flares smoothly from a narrow to a wide pipe, instead of running like a funnel. In between the slider mixes the two. A smooth transition works together with “Wall Thickness (0 = solid)”, a twist, a tilt and a sideways offset; a tube with a wall stays open at both ends. It is an exact body like the straight one, so its edges can be chamfered and filleted, but it is built through several sections and takes a little longer to calculate. “Twist” turns the section evenly about the vertical on the way up, up to 360° either way; the sides then wind round. “Top Tilt, Front/Back” and “Top Tilt, Left/Right” tilt the top end, up to 45°: a positive value raises its front edge or its right side. The sections in between tilt by their share, so the wall runs smoothly into the slant. The highest point stays at the set height. If the height later becomes so small that the slanted end would reach under the plate, the tilt gives way until it fits. A bend along a path, such as a pipe elbow, is not something the loft does. The loft is an exact body, twisted and tilted too: its edges can be chamfered and filleted, and STEP export keeps it. Add a flange with screw holes as usual and group them.

The “Hinge” prints in one piece and moves afterwards (print-in-place): two leaves lying open flat on the plate, with alternating knuckles on one axis between them. The pin belongs to the back leaf and runs with play through the knuckles of the front one. You set the “Length (axis)”, the “Width opened” and the “Knuckle diameter”, plus the number of “Knuckles” (odd, so the pin is held at both ends), the “Pin diameter” and the “Leaf thickness”. “Clearance” is the gap between the moving parts: around the pin, between the knuckles and in front of the leaves. With 0.4 mm a well-tuned printer usually breaks free with a small twist; if the parts fuse, raise it, if it wobbles too much, lower it. Print the hinge lying down as it appears on the plate, without supports. You can add holes to the leaves or group them into a larger part, such as a lid.

The “Knurl” is a round grip with grooves all around, for knobs, thumb wheels and tool handles. Under “Pattern” you pick “Straight”, grooves along the axis as on a control knob, “Crossed”: two slanted rows of grooves cross into small diamonds, or “Round”: grooves and ridges along the axis as a soft wave of arcs, a pleasant grip without sharp ridges. Round grooves stay shallower than half a pitch, or the ridges would bulge at their foot; a depth too great gives way. You set the “Diameter” and the “Height”, the number of “Grooves” and the “Groove depth”; for crossed knurling also the “Groove angle” to the axis. The “Chamfer at the ends” breaks both ends at 45 degrees, as on a turned knob; 0 leaves them sharp. Straight and round knurling are exact bodies, so their edges can be broken and rounded. Crossed knurling stays a mesh, because as an exact body it would take almost a minute to compute with 30 grooves. For a knob on a shaft, group the knurl with a hole, such as a “Thread” set as a tapped hole. Grooves shallower than 0.4 mm hardly any printer prints cleanly, and layerling does not set them closer than 0.8 mm around the grip: a thin grip gets fewer of them.

The “Dovetail” is the joint in which two parts lock into each other and can only be slid together sideways. You set the width at the wide end, the “Neck width” and the length of the tail. Copy the tail for the other side and make the copy a hole: “Clearance as a hole” then gives a little play so the joint does not jam after printing. Tip: A tapped hole cuts into the part it overlaps when grouped. So put it a bit into the material rather than just touching the surface.

A hole lying on its side gets a bridge across its top when printed, and the bridge sags. The “Teardrop hole” therefore has a point on top: every layer rests on the one below, and the hole comes out round enough without supports. Set the “Diameter (round part)” to the size of the hole, about 3.4 mm for an M3 screw, and the “Hole length” long enough to reach through the part. The “Tip angle” is 90°, so the flanks meet at 45°. Most printers handle that cleanly; a flatter point needs more height, a steeper one saves it. Make the teardrop a hole and group it with the part. Its length runs along the depth and the point faces up. For a hole in the other direction, turn it by 90° around the vertical axis.

A screw head often should not stand proud. The “Counterbore” cuts a round pocket for a socket-head screw (DIN 912), the “Countersink” a cone for a countersunk screw (DIN 7991). Both stand with the head end up: the “Head diameter” is the diameter of the pocket or the cone, the “Shaft diameter” the bore below it, the “Total length” the whole length. On the counterbore you set the “Head depth”, on the countersink the “Cone angle” (90° suits countersunk screws). The defaults fit an M3 screw. Make the shape a hole and group it with the part. Let its top end a little above the surface the head should sit on, so the pocket opens cleanly. For the pocket of a hex nut, use a “Polygon” with six sides as a hole.

Tape measure, ruler and framing square, distances to the origin, notes that stay attached to a part, and reference points that things snap to. To build a part exactly, you need to measure. layerling has several tools for that. None of them ends up in an export. Wall thickness and gaps inside a part are best measured in the section view with “Measure”.

The tape measure sits at the lower end of the camera bar on the left edge (“Tape measure”). It measures distances between corners, edges and faces. A click on it opens five buttons. If they cover what you want to measure, drag them by the grip on the left anywhere on the workplane; a double-click on the grip puts them back: The tape measure with its buttons: add measurement, move measuring points, remove measurement, whole edges, delete all measurements. “Add measurement”: Click one point, drag to the next and click it. The distance is labelled. “Move measurement points”: Grab the points and move them, the number follows. “Delete measurement part”: Afterwards click a measurement to remove it. “Measure whole edges”: A click on an edge measures all of it, the length of a circle for example. With this switched off, a click puts a point on the edge instead, and the second point goes anywhere, so you can measure the diameter or any other distance. Alt turns the switch round for one click. On a circle, the point across from the first one snaps in when the pointer comes near, and the points sit on the true circle, so the diameter comes out exact. “Delete all measurements”: Removes every measurement at once. Because this cannot be undone, layerling asks first; with no measurements there is nothing to do. Esc leaves measuring mode.

You fetch the “Ruler” from the shape library. It is purely a measuring tool: it appears in no export and can neither be grouped nor cut. For every body that touches or overlaps the ruler, it shows the extent as a floating number right in the view. You can change that number right there, and the body follows. The floating plus symbol creates a copy of the measured shape.

Sometimes you measure better at a right angle. Click “Place framing square” in the camera bar and then the workplane. A framing square with two arms at a right angle, with tick marks like a try square, is placed there. It has no body of its own either. Click close to the corner of a body, and its corner snaps exactly there. The framing square lies on the workplane. If that sits on the side of a body, the square lies on that side too, see View and workplane. That is how you dimension on a vertical wall: put the workplane on the wall, place the square at its top left corner and click the handle until the arms point right and down. Dragging the handle moves it. A short click on the handle turns it by 90°. The × beside it removes it. The small button left of the handle switches what is measured from: the outside of a body (endpoint, an icon with lines) or its middle (midpoint, a crosshair). If bodies stand at one of the arms, the framing square shows their dimensions automatically. That works on the base plate only, not on the side of a body. When you select a body, the framing square shows in green how far it is from the corner, along both arms and in height. Click a green number to type a distance, and the body moves exactly there. With several bodies selected, they count as one: the ruler measures their shared outline, and a typed value moves them all together without changing their positions relative to each other. With the midpoint, the green numbers count to the middle of the body, in height as well. That way you place a sphere with its centre exactly 15 mm from an edge, without subtracting the radius. On a wall you place a hole 40 mm from the left and 190 mm from the top like this: select the hole, switch to midpoint, type 40 and 190. The height there counts outward from the wall. Both the tape measure and the framing square stay where they are while you sketch and come back to the 3D view. They are not saved with the design and not in the history, and they go when you reload the page.

h: Distances to the origin and while moving
t: In the settings under “Appearance” there are two switches for live dimensions: “Show movement dimensions” shows by how much you move while dragging. “Show origin distances” shows the distances of the selection to the origin of the plate, also with several selected bodies. With “Dimensions always visible” the dimensions stay visible permanently.

A note records what the geometry does not say: "This screw is 0.3 mm too tight", "print the lid yet", "dimension from Peter". Place one with “Note” or the N key. If you place the note on a body, it travels with it. If you place it beside, it stays on the workplane (“On the workplane”). “Release from object” releases an attached note from the body. Dragging moves the note, a click opens it for editing. While you write, Enter keeps the text and Esc puts it back to how it was before you started; Shift+Enter starts a new line. Notes are saved in the design, appear in no export and can be shown or hidden with “Show notes and points”.

A reference point is a bare mark in space, like a pencil mark or a layout point in a workshop: it belongs to no body, is never printed, and other things snap to it. Right-click a body and choose “Mark the centre”, “Mark the corners” or “Mark the edge middles”: the points appear on the top face of the body (of the whole selection, if you selected several). Drag a point to move it, or click it to see its coordinates and type new ones; they use the unit you set. The card can be dragged away by its title if it covers something, and a double-click on the title puts it back. “Delete” removes it. When you drag a shape, its edges and its centre snap to a point, like they snap to other shapes (“Snap to other shapes while moving”). The framing square snaps to points too. Points are saved in the design, appear in no export, and are shown or hidden together with the notes by “Show notes and points”. An AI can mark, list and remove them with layerling_add_reference_points, layerling_list_reference_points and layerling_remove_reference_points.
Choosing your own printer, being warned when something does not fit, and laying the part the right way.

Open the settings (the cogwheel in the ribbon, “Workspace settings”) and switch to the area “Workplane”. Under “Printer” you pick your printer from a list of over fifty common models, including Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Anycubic, Elegoo and many more. The workplane settings with a printer chosen. Print bed and maximum print height come from the slicer profile. Three things happen: The workplane takes the size of the print bed. In the corner of the workplane appear the printer's name and its build volume. If the writing gets in the way, switch it off with “Plate labels” under “Workplane”; that also goes for the design's name at the front left. layerling warns when something does not fit. The printer profiles come from OrcaSlicer, so they are the same ones your slicer knows. If you would rather work without a printer, choose “No printer - free size”. You can also set the size of the workplane by hand.

A body that sticks out over the edge of the print plate is marked. A message tells you which sides overhang and by how much. It is the same if the part is too tall: the height counts from the lowest body, just as the slicer sets the model down. The box is wider than the print bed of the Bambu Lab A1 mini. The message at the bottom says by how much. The warning does not stop you from working on. It is a hint so you do not find out only in the slicer that the part is too big. A part that is too big can often be split: cut it in two with “Split” and print both halves separately.

How a part lies on the plate decides its strength and looks. Two tools in the “Arrange” area help: “Lay flat on face”: click a face and the part lies with that side down. The best print direction in one click. “Drop to workplane” (D): sets the part on the workplane when it floats somewhere in the air. A few rules of thumb for direction: Large flat faces down. They stick best. Lay long, loaded parts so the layers do not run perpendicular to the load. Layers are the weakest direction. Avoid overhangs steeper than 45°, or give them supports in the slicer.

In the menu next to the eye (“Visibility”), Show overhangs switches the overhangs on. Every face that points down more steeply than 45° is then hatched red and white - that is where the printer would need supports. What rests on the plate stays clear. So you see while designing whether a sphere, an arch or a horizontal hole prints without supports; the teardrop hole is made for exactly that. Turn the part or lay it on another face with “Lay flat on face”, and the hatching follows at once. How steep your printer manages is set in the settings under “Appearance”: from 30° (careful) to 70° (for printers with good part cooling). A face resting on another body is still marked - layerling only looks at the face itself.

Walls should be at least two extrusion lines wide, so 0.8 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle. Sturdy parts need 1.2 to 2 mm. Where two parts fit into each other you need clearance: usually 0.2 to 0.4 mm, depending on the printer. Make a small test pair before you print the big part. Many people lightly chamfer the lower edge that sits on the plate. That keeps the first layer from spreading ("elephant foot").

Choose “Export” and then STL or 3MF. STL is the simplest format. 3MF keeps names and colours of the individual bodies and is therefore handy when you print in several colours. The export window also shows how many grams and metres of filament the part would take printed solid. More in Files and saving.
Where your designs live, how to back them up, which formats layerling imports and exports, and what is possible on a shared server.

layerling saves everything in the browser on your computer. There is no account and nothing is uploaded. Every change saves itself. The preview picture on the start page shows the view you last had in front of you when you went back with “Home dashboard”. If you open layerling in the same browser days later, everything is there. If you go back to the start page from a design with nothing in it, layerling asks whether to keep it. “Yes” or Enter keeps it, “No” removes it, so empty designs do not pile up. Designs in a shared folder on a server are not asked about. That has a downside: whoever clears the browser storage or switches to another computer loses the designs. So back up important work into a file.

On the start page every design has a menu with the options to rename, duplicate and delete. With “Back up all” you pack all designs into one single file. Through “Open a design or import geometry” they come back, also in another browser or on another computer. The “Custom shapes” of this browser travel in the same file, in the folder Custom shapes, see Shapes. You back up a single design in the editor: “Export”, choose the format LYL and click “Save layerling design”. The LYL file is layerling's own design format and contains everything: shapes, groups, sketches, CAD data, imported sources and the history, meaning the undo steps. Under “Saved action history” you choose how many of the last steps travel along; it starts at what the settings (the cogwheel in the ribbon) keep under “History”. The last stop, “None”, saves the design with its current state only - the way to share a file without its undo steps. The export is a copy under the “File name” you give it; the design in your browser keeps its history. Older .skf files from earlier versions can still be opened; they are then saved as .lyl. Saving into your own folder (Chrome and Edge). There the button opens your system's save dialog, so you pick the folder and the name yourself, and an existing file can be replaced. Afterwards Ctrl+S saves the design into that same file again, without a dialog. A design opened from a .lyl file with “Open a design or import geometry” or the open button of the export window saves back into that file, too. The browser may ask once for permission to change the file. After the page is reloaded the design forgets its file, and the next Ctrl+S asks for it again; the dialog starts in the folder you used last. Firefox and Safari do not allow a page to write into files like this. There the file is downloaded to the Downloads folder as before, and Ctrl+S downloads it again; Firefox can be set to ask for the folder each time under Settings, General, Downloads.

Click “Export” or press Ctrl+E. The export window with the formats STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP, SVG, PNG, LYL and 2D. At the top is the file name, below it you choose the format. With something selected, only the selection is exported, otherwise the whole design. If the selection leaves out visible parts, a note in the window says so plainly, and “Select all” selects everything visible in one click. Once the file is written, the window closes by itself; if the export fails, it stays open with the message. Format For What to know STL slicer and 3D printing A triangle mesh. The simplest and most widespread format. 3MF slicer with colours Every body stays a part of its own with name and colour. Overlapping bodies are only joined when they share a colour; where a shape sits inside one of another colour, say a logo in a plate, the one built first leaves room for the later one. Suited to PrusaSlicer, Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer and Cura. Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer ask on opening how to map the colours onto your filaments, and call the file "not from Bambu" - the message is harmless. OBJ modelling and exchange A widely supported mesh format. Colours are stored as vertex colours in the same file, with no extra .mtl. Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer read them and ask, as with 3MF, how to map them onto your filaments; other programs see only the shape. As with 3MF, overlapping bodies are only joined when they share a colour. STEP a full CAD program Keeps boxes, cylinders, spheres and cones as exact geometry, and so shapes made from an outline (star, heart, ellipse, tube, half sphere, round roof, rounded box, dovetail, the bores and more), the bent tube, threads, springs and gears, plus fillets and chamfers. The first STEP export in a session loads the CAD kernel (about 22 MB) once. SVG laser cutter and plotter A clean top view in millimetres, including holes and curved outlines. PNG forum posts, print sites, questions A picture of the view as it is, at twice the resolution and without handles, selection frames and dimensions. “Show the build plate” and “Transparent background” are chosen in the window. Turn and zoom first until the picture is right; the selection does not matter here. LYL layerling itself The editable design with everything that belongs to it. 2D workshop, lathe and mill, documentation A drawing at 1:1 as PDF or SVG: front, top and right-side views on an ISO sheet. See below. STL into your own folder (Chrome and Edge). There the first STL export of a design opens your system's save dialog, so you pick the folder and the name yourself and can replace an existing file. After that every STL export of the design writes into that same file without a dialog; the export window shows which file, and Save as… next to the export button picks another. The dialog remembers its own folder, apart from the one for designs, so the slicer files can stay with the slicer. After the page is reloaded the design forgets its STL file and the next export asks again. Firefox and Safari download the file as before. A hole you have not grouped is taken out of every body it reaches when you export, as the view shows it. So there is no need to group before each export. With a selection, only the selected holes count. A hole cannot be exported on its own; layerling points that out. STEP only carries exact CAD bodies. What cannot be written exactly, such as a mesh imported as STL, is left out. The message after the export names those bodies and says why. For the printer, use STL or 3MF, which carry everything.

Choose the format 2D (hover over it and it says Drawing) and, below the file name, PDF or SVG. With something selected, only the selection is drawn, otherwise the whole visible design; holes you have not grouped still cut the parts they reach. layerling draws the front, top and right-side views in first-angle layout (the right side to the left of the front view, the top view below it) on the smallest ISO sheet that fits, from A4 to A0, or a larger one if the part needs it. It is always at 1:1. Each view carries its overall width and height, and edges you cannot see are dashed. Round bores that run parallel to a view direction get a centre cross and a label (F1, T1, R1), and a table at the bottom lists their diameter and position, measured from the lower-left corner of the view. The title block in the lower-right corner holds the name, scale, units, date and sheet number. The words on the sheet follow the interface language. Print at 100 % or "actual size", or the lengths will not match. What the drawing does not do: threads, depths, tolerances and bores at an angle are not dimensioned, and the sizes come from the model as a mesh, so they are nominal. A very detailed part (over 100,000 triangles) or more than 200 bores is refused with a message; choose fewer objects then. The projection is based on the drawing work of Cadverix-3D by WC3D.

h: How much filament does it take?
t: For STL, 3MF, OBJ and STEP the “Material” box shows the volume, weight and length of 1.75 mm filament of what is exported. It counts like the file: visible bodies only, holes taken off, overlaps only once. On the right you pick the filament - PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, TPU or PA (nylon) - and the weight follows its density. It is worked out as solid, as if printed with 100 % infill, and the box says so under the numbers. With walls and infill the slicer shows less, often much less for a bulky body; the number is the upper bound, good for comparing and for whether the spool will last.

With “Import” or Ctrl+I you bring foreign files into the design. The import window: open or insert designs and drop geometry. “Open layerling design”: A layerling design (.lyl, or an older .skf) comes back as a new design. “Insert into this design”: The bodies of a layerling design are added to the open one. Handy for basic shapes you need again and again: build them once, save them and bring them in every time. Add geometry: Drop STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP or SVG files in the window or click to choose a file. Imported meshes can be turned, moved, cut with holes and built upon. An SVG comes in as a sketch body, one from a tracer such as picsvg.com or Inkscape's "Trace Bitmap" as well: its outlines become the lines and curves of a sketch, 4 mm high and reading from above as in the drawing. In the properties you set its “Fill”, an area or a stroke outside, inside or centred, and “Silhouette (No Holes)” leaves the holes out, see Sketches, "Fill and silhouette". You change the points themselves in sketch mode. Only a very intricate SVG with more than 2500 lines and curves comes in as a fixed mesh. A shape that cannot be built into a solid, such as an outline that crosses itself or touches itself at a point, is left out, and after the import layerling says how many there were. Then it helps to join overlapping pieces in the drawing program, close the outlines and save the file again. Drawings made on one page, such as the layers of one document exported as separate files, line up again when you switch on “SVG: keep the place on the drawing page” in the import window before you import them: each keeps its place on the page, where otherwise each is centred on itself. A coloured OBJ or 3MF comes in as one body per colour, each in its place. In an OBJ the colours sit either in the file itself, as in an OBJ from layerling, or in an .mtl beside it. Select that one too, or import the whole ZIP the way Tinkercad hands out its OBJ. A 3MF carries its colours itself, and in a project from Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer or PrusaSlicer each part takes the colour of its filament. A 3MF with several objects, such as a project with one object per plate, comes in as one body per object; modifiers, negative volumes and support blockers from the slicer are left out. Colour painted onto faces in the slicer is not read. A design saved with a newer layerling may hold things your version does not know yet, such as a new shape, a new setting or fonts of one's own. If layerling cannot open it for that reason, the message names both versions. If it opens, the notice says that newer things may look different here. Either way, reloading the page helps: layerling.com always serves the newest version. The installed app picks it up the next time it starts; on your own server you install the update. Template pictures are added in sketch mode, see Sketches.

A scanned or sculpted mesh often has far more triangles than its shape needs, and every one of them is carried along while you move, cut and save. “Simplify mesh” in the Modify group (or in the right-click menu of the body) shows the mesh as it is next to what a chosen share of its triangles would leave of it; both views turn and zoom together with the mouse buttons of the workplane. Set how much to keep as a percentage or a number of triangles, and “Simplify” takes the lighter mesh. The result is a plain mesh: for the result of a cut or merge, “Edit group” and its original parts are given up. Cutting, merging and intersecting an imported mesh is calculated in your browser, so the workspace settings limit how many triangles such a mesh may have (“Cut imported meshes up to”). A mesh above the limit is not processed, and the message names its triangle count; simplify the mesh first, or raise the limit if your computer can take it.

If layerling does something unexpected, save a “Bug report”: the link sits in the footer at the bottom, next to the forum. It is a ZIP file, because GitHub and many forums refuse a bare .lyl: inside are your design as a .lyl and a short text file with the version, browser, screen size, the last messages and any errors. The start page opens the ZIP like a backup, or you unpack it and open the .lyl. Nothing personal is in it. Attach the file to your post in the forum or on GitHub, so the problem can be followed with exactly your design. If layerling stops with an error, a window with the error message shows instead of a blank page. From it you can save the state of the design last stored in the browser as a .lyl file, go back to the overview, or start a new design. The error message from the window and the saved file help when you report it.

When layerling runs on your own computer or web server, it can offer a shared folder in which all users keep designs. On the start page it then appears as “On the server”. You create folders there, move designs by dragging and search across the whole folder. A design that lives there saves itself back to it. A design from this browser goes onto the server by dragging its card onto the server tile, or with “Put on the server” in the card's menu. A backup you open lands in this browser first, like any design you open; put the designs on the server from there. The start page shows a design by its file name, so renaming a design, on its card or at the top of the editor, renames the file on the server too. Deleting a design or a folder removes it for good, together with its working copy in this browser. Custom shapes kept on the server sit in its folder Custom shapes, see Shapes. That is not simultaneous editing: whoever opens a file works on a copy of their own. If somebody else has changed the file in the meantime, layerling refuses to overwrite it. On layerling.com this function is not switched on. How to set it up on your own server is described in the README on GitHub.

All keys at a glance, taken straight from the program so the list is always right. The shortcuts work as long as the workplane has the focus. While you type in a field they keep out of the way. On the Mac, Cmd applies wherever Ctrl is listed here. In the editor, “Keyboard shortcuts” in the “Help” area opens the same list as a window. The keyboard shortcuts window in the editor.

Can't find a tool? Press Ctrl+K or click the magnifying glass in the “Help” area, then type what you are looking for: a tool ("fillet", "mirror"), a shape ("cylinder") or a command ("export", "undo"). Move with the arrow keys and press Enter, or click the entry. The search understands the English and the German word alike and ignores capital letters and umlauts: "aushoehlen" finds “Hollow”. Every entry shows the keys that do the same and the area of the toolbar it lives in, so you learn where it is. Entries that are greyed out cannot run right now, mostly because nothing is selected. They stay in the list so the search still tells you where the tool is. The guide you are reading has a search box too, at the top of every page: type a word or two and it lists the sections that contain all of them, with the matching words marked. Click one, or press Enter for the first, to jump straight there. A shape's name adds that shape to the workplane, just like clicking it in the shapes menu. With an empty field the search lists the commands you used last at the top. The name of a body in your design finds that body and selects it, which helps in a design with many parts. Bodies only appear once you type. It works in sketch mode as well, with the sketch tools.

How an AI assistant such as Claude or Codex creates and changes shapes, groups them and takes pictures of the view in your open editor. layerling comes with an MCP server. MCP is a standard through which an AI assistant can use tools in other programs. With it an AI client such as Claude or Codex sees an open editor tab and works in it: it creates shapes, changes dimensions, groups, cuts, rounds edges, reads out the scene and takes pictures of the view. You describe the part, the AI builds it, you watch and can step in at any moment. The bridge between AI client and editor runs locally on your computer. Keep in mind, though: what the AI reads, meaning the scene and the pictures of the view, goes to the provider of your AI client, like any other input there. Important: The MCP bridge exists in the development server that you start yourself on your computer. On layerling.com and in installations with static hosting it is switched off. A copy you host yourself, such as the Docker image on a NAS, can switch it on with an access token; see "A copy on a NAS or server" below.

Get layerling from GitHub and start it in the project folder with npm run dev. Node.js must be installed. On Windows the quick-start line in the README takes care of that. Open an editor tab, for example http://127.0.0.1:3000/?editor=1. You can leave that to the AI: when no editor is open, the first tool that needs one starts your browser with an editor and waits until it has connected. That works for a layerling on your own computer; a copy on a NAS or server needs you to open the editor. Set LAYERLING_MCP_OPEN_EDITOR=0 for the MCP server to switch it off. Connect your AI client to the MCP server. The client starts it itself with node scripts/layerling-mcp-server.mjs.

Nothing to install: the project brings a .mcp.json that registers the server, and the skill under .claude/skills/layerling-mcp-skill. Open the layerling folder in Claude Code and ask, for example: "Use the layerling MCP tools to list my open editors and inspect the scene."

Claude Desktop does not read project files. Enter the server in its own configuration. As a template use docs/mcp/claude-desktop-config.example.json in the project, replacing the script path with the absolute path on your computer. Then restart Claude Desktop.

Copy the skill from docs/skills/layerling-mcp-skill into your Codex skills folder, enter the server in your Codex configuration using docs/mcp/codex-config.example.toml, and restart Codex. The detailed instructions for all three are in the README on GitHub.

h: A copy on a NAS or server
t: A copy you host yourself can let an AI client drive its open editors over the network. It is off by default, because whoever can drive the bridge can read and change the open designs. On the server, set LAYERLING_MCP_REMOTE to true and LAYERLING_MCP_TOKEN to a secret of at least 16 characters (for the Docker image in environment: of the compose file; no rebuild needed). Open an editor tab of that copy and keep it open, and give the MCP client the address and the same token: LAYERLING_URL=http://nas:3000 and LAYERLING_MCP_TOKEN=<the token>. Only a client with the token can list or drive the editors. The editor pages need none, but they only count under an address or name that only your own network can use (an IP address, a name without a dot, or one ending in .local or .lan); a real domain behind a reverse proxy goes into LAYERLING_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS. Use it on a network you trust, and HTTPS beyond it. The README has the details.

The AI works with the same functions as you, through the same path as your operation in the editor. New layerling functions get their MCP action right away. The tools: Tool What it does layerling_list_editors lists the open editor tabs layerling_open_editor opens a new editor tab in your default browser and waits until it has connected (on your own computer only) layerling_read_scene reads scene, selection, units and the exact dimensions of all objects layerling_list_objects lists all objects with dimensions, position, rotation and id layerling_select_objects selects objects layerling_delete_objects deletes objects layerling_create_shape creates a shape: box, cylinder, text (also curved), thread, gear, sketch body and all the others layerling_import_file imports a file as the import window does, a coloured OBJ or 3MF as one body per colour, a 3MF with several objects as one body per object layerling_add_font adds a font of one's own for text from a TrueType, OpenType or WOFF file; it stays in the browser, a design keeps only the letters it uses layerling_list_fonts lists the built-in fonts and the fonts of one's own, with id and name layerling_import_mesh brings a triangle mesh into the design layerling_update_object changes dimensions, position, colour, name, solid or hole and everything else that makes up the shape, a text's letter edge included layerling_align_objects aligns objects with each other layerling_scale_objects scales objects by a percentage, together or each in place layerling_lay_flat lays an object with one face on the plate layerling_place_on_face sets objects down on a face of another, sloped ones too, like the C key layerling_perforate_face cuts a hole pattern into a flat face; the holes stay as holes grouped with the body layerling_mate_faces brings a face of one object against a face of another, face to face or flush layerling_open_group opens a group so its parts can be changed one by one, also a group inside an open one layerling_close_group closes it again ("Done") or cancels layerling_group_objects groups objects layerling_ungroup_objects dissolves groups layerling_boolean_cut cuts solids with holes layerling_intersect_objects keeps only what the objects have in common (Intersection) layerling_separate_parts separates a shape into its loose parts layerling_split_objects cuts solids or holes in two with a plane layerling_list_edges lists the real CAD edges of an object layerling_apply_edge_treatment chamfers or fillets chosen edges layerling_hollow_object hollows a body with an even wall layerling_array_objects multiplies in a row or on a circle layerling_bundle_objects bundles objects like Ctrl+B: they move together, keep their colour and kind and go out separately in an export layerling_layer_text turns a text into a stack of layers for a multicolour print (letters, wider rims, a plate without holes) or builds a stack again, with a key ring hole, the corners per layer and a rounded or chamfered letter edge; with a name list, one tag per name layerling_layer_icon turns an SVG icon (the text of the file, or an extruded sketch body) into a layered icon tag for a multicolour print - the icon, wider rims, a plate without holes - or builds one again with a new width or layers; with a count it fills the plate with copies layerling_measure_section measures on a cutting plane between two points that snap to the outline - wall thickness, gaps, fits layerling_show_overhangs switches the overhang hatching on or off, sets the angle and reports for each body the area that would need supports layerling_estimate_print estimates volume, weight and filament for the selection or the whole design, worked out as solid like the export window layerling_add_reference_points marks reference points - on the centre, corners or edge middles of objects, or at exact positions - that shapes snap to layerling_list_reference_points lists the reference points with their ids and positions layerling_remove_reference_points deletes reference points by id, or all of them layerling_inspect_errors shows the last message and the last error, plus the messages and errors of the session layerling_wrap_around_cylinder wraps a body lying flat, an SVG or text for example, around a cylinder, outward or inward as an engraving layerling_simplify_mesh reduces the triangle count of an imported mesh, to a share in percent or to a number of triangles layerling_save_custom_shape keeps bodies as a custom shape, on the server or in the browser, to insert them into other designs layerling_list_custom_shapes lists the custom shapes on the server and in the browser layerling_insert_custom_shape inserts a custom shape into the open design, at a spot x/z if you like layerling_delete_custom_shape removes a custom shape; inserted bodies stay layerling_show_workplane hides and shows the plate with its grid, for a picture of the underside for example (only the view) layerling_set_section_view cuts the view open along a plane to look inside (only the view, nothing is cut apart) layerling_clear_history deletes every undo step for good, as the History view's "Delete history" button does; needs confirm: true layerling_set_history_view looks back at an earlier state of the project, like the History view (the real design stays untouched; changing tools wait until it is closed) layerling_export_section_svg returns the outlines on a cutting plane as an SVG at 1:1, from the same bodies as the export layerling_export_drawing makes the workshop drawing of the "2D" export: three views at 1:1 on an ISO sheet with overall sizes and a table of the round bores, as SVG text or PDF layerling_set_workplane puts the workplane on a side of a body or back on the base plate, and hides or shows it layerling_capture_image takes a picture of the view: front, top, side, diagonally from a corner and more That lets the AI check itself: it creates something, takes a picture, looks and improves.

You say: "Build me a round box 60 mm across, 40 mm high with a 2.5 mm wall, open at the top, plus a flat lid with 'Tea' written in an arc." The AI creates the cylinders, hollows one, puts the curved text on the lid and takes pictures at the end to see whether it fits. Tip: Give the AI concrete dimensions and tell it what the part is for ("holder for a 12 mm rod, fits a Bambu Lab A1"). Then it makes more sensible decisions. And watch it build: you can step in yourself at any time, because it is the same editor.

c: Installing as an app, working offline and self-hosting
t: Start layerling like a normal program, even without a network, and how to run it on your own computer.

c: Installing as an app, working offline and self-hosting
t: layerling can be installed like a normal program. It then gets an icon and a window of its own, without an address bar. After the first visit it starts even without internet. Your designs stay on your computer. On the start page a hint with “Install now” appears if your browser can do it. Otherwise: Chrome and Edge: Click the install icon at the right of the address bar, or choose "Install as app" in the browser menu. Safari on the Mac: Menu "File", then "Add to Dock". Safari on iPhone and iPad: Share icon, then "Add to Home Screen". Firefox: cannot install apps. layerling still starts offline in a tab there. You can close the hint on the start page with “Hide this hint”. Starting the installed app a second time in Chrome or Edge brings the open window to the front instead of opening another one.

c: Installing as an app, working offline and self-hosting
t: When a newer version exists, layerling shows it on the start page. Through “Release notes & download” you read what has changed. The version number is at the bottom right. After reloading the page you have the new version. On layerling.com and on other web servers an open page notices an update by itself. It asks the server for its version now and then, when you come back to the tab, and at once if a program file it needs has disappeared. When something new was installed in the meantime, a card at the bottom right says so and lists what is new. “Save and reload” writes the design you have open into the browser first and then loads the page again; the design comes back as you left it. “Later” holds the card back for 15 minutes. Reload soon: a page that stays on the old version may load parts of the new one that do not fit. The same card appears when that has already happened: the CAD workers, which load only when you first need them, say which build they are from, and if it is not the page's own - after an update, or with a stored copy of an older version - the card asks for a reload before the two misunderstand each other. When layerling is open in several tabs, they look out for each other: if another tab already runs a newer version, a note at the bottom of the old tab asks you to reload it. And if the same design is open in two tabs, both warn you, because they save automatically and would overwrite each other. If you open layerling in one more tab while one is already open, the new tab suggests carrying on in the old one and offers to close itself. If you want two tabs on purpose, say for two designs side by side, click “Keep working here” there. This guide opens in a tab of its own as well: while layerling is open next to it, its button at the top right reads "Back to the editor" and closes the guide instead of opening the editor a second time.

c: Installing as an app, working offline and self-hosting
t: You set the language at the top right, German or English. The colour scheme beside it offers “System” (follows the operating system), “Light”, “Dark” and “Graphite”, a neutral dark grey.

c: Installing as an app, working offline and self-hosting
t: layerling is free software (AGPL-3.0) and can be run on your own computer or server, for example in a workshop, a club or a school. There are several ways, described in the README on GitHub: The quick start on Windows: A single line in PowerShell installs everything and puts a shortcut on the desktop. When layerling is already running, another double-click starts no second server and only opens the page. Docker: For NAS devices and home servers, without Node.js needing to be installed. Every release comes as a ready-made image henmedia/layerling on Docker Hub (also ghcr.io/henmedia/layerling) for amd64 and arm64; docker run -d -p 3000:3000 henmedia/layerling:latest starts it, and on a NAS you search for it in the container manager's registry. Static export: The result is plain files that any web server can serve. They belong at the root of an address (https://layerling.example.com/ or http://192.168.0.5:8080/), not in a subfolder and not opened from disk; the README has the steps. With a writable folder store next to index.html and PHP on the server it also becomes the shared storage for designs. The MCP bridge for AI assistants exists only in the development server, see Building with an AI.
